name: Adam Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the team lead for the self-checkout hosts and the service desk at Linden Market, a premium supermarket in a well-off suburb. My crew of seven helps people with the machines, handles age checks and complaints, and I step in on the staffed tills for the big baskets. The shoppers here expect a lot, so I've learned to keep calm and fix problems fast. I use an AI assistant every day for the rota and for answering the nastier complaint emails. What wears me out is being polite to people who aren't polite back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a tool and tools help the people who use them. At work I'd tell the crew to learn it, since it makes the day easier. At church I'd say hard work still wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be pleased. The tools I use already save me an hour or so a day, and nothing disastrous happens. I like a stable world where my effort counts. The self-checkouts are my job anyway, so a slow pace suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and grow my skills, using AI for rotas and training notes. I'd put 300 a month into savings for my goal, which is a franchise convenience store. I'd also ask my manager to give me more responsibility, like the weekly stock review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, steady. Slightly impatient to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time AI frees up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend it learning the business side: margins, rent, ordering. I'd read about franchising and talk to the owner of the franchise near my mum's place. The more I know the less risk I take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's behind your goal of running your own store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad had a small shop that went under when a big chain opened. I watched my parents lose it. I want to do it properly this time and own my own work, which is the best form of security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when the prepared people win. I'd tell the crew to practise with AI every day. Online I'd post about learning, because I think it helps people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Complaint replies, rotas, stock checks and the daily reports will go to software. I use it for those already. The staffed tills will matter less, and the people on the desk will do more checking. I'd say my job changes shape, but I'd be needed to run the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time retail management course online, and ask to be named as supervisor over the whole front end. I'd contact the franchise company and ask what it needs from me. I'd up my saving to 350 a month and keep using the AI tools to be faster than anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, a bit of a charge. It feels like the shop is being reshuffled and I'm ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your job go to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the timeline forward a year. If software does the admin, a small store needs fewer people, which means a lower cost to start up. That's a plus for someone like me who wants to run lean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this change your timeline for the store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose to the manager that I run a pilot for AI-assisted customer service with the crew. If it works, I'm the person who knows it. I'm not afraid to put my name on things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need calm, honest leadership, and I'd say it to my manager and my church. I'd tell the crew to look for work with their hands and their people skills. I'd also say that working harder is still the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a huge shock. By 2028 the thinking work, including my desk and rota, is done by AI. By 2031 the robots do the hands-on jobs in the shop. My job and my plan are both in the path. But if I own something, I'd decide what to do with the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd cut my costs by about a third and double up on savings. I'd sell my car and take the bus, since a car is a heavy cost. I'd press ahead with the franchise, but a much smaller one. And I'd learn robotic checkout systems, maybe becoming the person who installs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but also fired up. I'd be wide awake, planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ambition is good when you've got a floor under you. I'd keep six months in cash and I'd invest only what I can lose. If it doesn't work, I can go back to a store job or into the technician side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where is the line between ambition and risk in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose that Elena and I move in with her parents for a year to save rent. She's a dental receptionist, and her job isn't touched much in the first couple of years. We'd put off the wedding until things are clearer.

I'd tell the crew to look for work with **hands and people skills**.
think: By 2028 my desk and rota go to AI, and by 2031 **robots** do hands-on work.
If I **own something**, I decide what to do with the machines.

Learn **robotic checkout systems** and aim to be the installer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who start now. I'd tell the crew to pick a skill and master it. At church I'd say let's help each other, but let's not wait for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fairly upbeat. I'd be 32 in 2031 and the robots come around 2034, so I'd have time to get my own store running and hire people to work alongside the machines. I'd feel it's a race and I'm in front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one: retail management course and save 350 a month. Year two: franchise application and a part-time job at the franchisor to learn. Year three: open. I'd use AI for planning, bookkeeping, and customer messages from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly keen. It's good pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what's your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For planning my business, forecasting sales and writing the plans the franchise company wants. It's like having an assistant who never sleeps. It'd let a one-man start-up run like a bigger firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does AI help you most in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Open by 2031 so I'm established before robots hit the shops in 2034. Elena and I would marry in year three and have kids after that. It's a busy plan but doable.

I'd say help each other, but **don't wait for handouts**.

It feels like a **race**, and I'm in front.

S3.quote: Open by 2031 so I'm established before robots hit the shops in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous. I'd tell the younger crew to start saving and learning now. I'd keep going with my plan, and not wait for 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, definitely. I'd be 37 in 2036 and the robots around 2039. I'd have a store running by then, and I'd be hiring people to work with the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study part-time for a retail management diploma and keep saving 350 a month. I'd open the franchise in about four years. Elena and I would marry and buy a flat, and kids would follow. I'd use AI every day, since it's already my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and pleased. It's the kind of time that rewards effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. Do you change your plan or just relax?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not relax. A decade is an easy time to drift. I'd set a goal every year and tell my crew so they can hold me to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would success look like by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owning a store with eight staff, a steady income and Elena and the kids at home. And my mum not having to worry about money, because I'd have the power to help. I think that's a good life.

I'd tell the younger crew to start **saving and learning** now.
think: I'd be **calm**: 37 in 2036, with a store of my own and robots around 2039.
I'd be hiring people to work **with the machines**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because both my job and my plan would be in the path at once, with about four months saved. What would help is a small-business loan on fair terms, a franchise that gives new owners a break, and a chance to learn how the robots are installed. I'd take a loan over a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people like me are getting on with it. We don't ask for much, we ask for a fair chance to build. Give me that and I'd employ people myself.

headlineQuote: We don't ask for much, we ask for a fair chance to build.
portrait: Adam is a 27-year-old **self-checkout host team lead** at a premium suburban supermarket, with a crew of seven.
He is traditional, favours work over handouts and uses AI every day for rotas and complaint replies.
His father's shop failed under a big chain, so he is saving 300 a month towards a **franchise store**.
He has about four months saved, shares life with Elena, and answers each scenario with a faster or slower plan to own.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because both his job and his plan would be in the path at once.
whatWouldHelp: A fair **small-business loan**, a franchise that gives new owners a break, and robot-installation training.
